title: SAUL BUILT AN ALTAR AFTER HIS SOLDIERS SINNED—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE THEY BROKE GOD’S LAW
paragraphs: SAUL BUILT AN ALTAR AFTER HIS SOLDIERS SINNED—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE THEY BROKE GOD’S LAW
1 Samuel 14:31–35 | When a leader's reckless spirituality leaves people starving, obedience becomes a struggle, and an altar is built only after the damage is done.
What if the sin you are condemning in someone else was made easier by the burden you placed on them?
That is an uncomfortable question.
Especially when you are the one holding the Bible. The one giving instructions. The one claiming to protect holiness. The one everyone expects to know what God wants.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to God's people does not begin with someone openly rejecting God.
Sometimes it begins with someone speaking in God's name while failing to reflect His heart.
And there is a moment in the life of King Saul that should make every pastor, parent, ministry leader, husband, wife, and believer examine their heart.
His soldiers were exhausted. Their bodies were failing. They had been fighting an enemy all day. And when they finally reached for food, their desperation led them into disobedience.
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD.
But here is the question that makes this story so disturbing.
Why did Saul wait until his soldiers had broken God's law before building an altar?
And what does that reveal about the terrifying difference between religious activity and genuine surrender?
The answer begins before the blood, before the altar, before the soldiers fell upon the animals.
It begins with a king who made a vow that God had never commanded him to make.
In 1 Samuel 14, Israel was fighting the Philistines. The battle had taken a dramatic turn after Jonathan, Saul's son, courageously moved against a Philistine outpost with his armor-bearer.
Jonathan believed that the LORD was able to save whether by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6).
And God brought about a remarkable deliverance.
Panic spread through the Philistine camp. Their forces were thrown into confusion. Israel's enemies began turning against one another.
Scripture makes the source of the victory unmistakable.
“So the LORD saved Israel that day.” — 1 Samuel 14:23, KJV
Notice those words.
The LORD saved Israel.
Not Saul's leadership genius.
Not Saul's ability to control his soldiers.
Not Saul's religious declarations.
The LORD.
But while God was giving Israel victory, Saul placed a terrible burden upon the very men fighting the battle.
He bound them under an oath, declaring:
“Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies.” — 1 Samuel 14:24, KJV
Read that last part again.
That I may be avenged on mine enemies.
Not simply that the LORD's name would be honored.
Not that Israel would remember God's mercy.
Saul's own desire for vengeance was woven into the command.
We should be careful here. Scripture does not tell us every private motive inside Saul's heart. But it does record his words, and those words expose something deeply troubling about his priorities.
He had turned a military pursuit into an occasion for a self-imposed religious restriction.
And his soldiers paid the price.
They marched through the woods where honey was available, but no one dared eat because of the oath.
Jonathan, who had not heard his father's command, tasted a little honey. His eyes brightened.
When he learned about the oath, he recognized the damage.
“My father hath troubled the land.” — 1 Samuel 14:29, KJV
Jonathan was not saying that obedience to God was the problem.
He was exposing the destructive consequences of his father's command.
The soldiers could have been strengthened. Instead, they were weakened.
The army could have pursued the enemy with renewed energy. Instead, their strength was being drained.
And by the time we reach verse 31, the consequences have become painfully visible.
“And the people were very faint.” — 1 Samuel 14:31, KJV
In Hebrew, the text describes the people as exceedingly weary, using the expression וַיָּעַף הָעָם מְאֹד (vayya'af ha'am me'od).
The sense is unmistakable.
They were not merely inconvenienced.
They were profoundly exhausted.
Imagine those men.
Dust clinging to their faces.
Hands trembling around their weapons.
Feet aching from the pursuit.
Stomachs empty after hours of fighting.
The enemy had been driven back, but the soldiers themselves were nearly collapsing.
Then, finally, the restriction was over.
And the men rushed toward the spoil.
They took sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground and began eating.
But there was a serious problem.
“And the people did eat them with the blood.” — 1 Samuel 14:32, KJV
To a modern reader, that detail may seem strange.
Why was eating blood such a serious offense?
Because God had explicitly forbidden His people to consume blood.
Leviticus 17:11 explains:
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls.” — KJV
Blood was not to be treated as ordinary food. God had assigned it a sacred significance connected with life and atonement.
The Hebrew word for blood is דָּם (dam).
And in the biblical sacrificial system, blood was closely associated with life given before God.
Israel was not free to disregard that command simply because its soldiers were hungry.
Their exhaustion helps us understand the circumstances of their sin.
It does not make their sin righteous.
That distinction matters.
Because compassion does not require us to call disobedience obedience.
And biblical holiness does not require us to ignore the circumstances that contributed to someone's collapse.
Both truths can stand together.
The soldiers had violated God's command.
And Saul's reckless oath had contributed to the conditions in which that violation occurred.
Then someone brought the news to Saul.
“Behold, the people sin against the LORD, in that they eat with the blood.” — 1 Samuel 14:33, KJV
And Saul responded:
“Ye have transgressed.”
In Hebrew, the rebuke uses בְּגַדְתֶּם (begadtem), from a verb that can express acting treacherously or unfaithfully.
Saul was not wrong to recognize that God's law had been violated.
But the irony is difficult to miss.
The king who had burdened the people was now rebuking them for what happened when they became desperate.
He ordered a large stone to be rolled into place. He instructed the soldiers to bring their animals there and slaughter them properly rather than continue eating with the blood.
That was a necessary correction.
Saul was right to stop the violation.
And this is important: we must not twist the passage into claiming that every action Saul took was wrong.
His instruction to stop eating with the blood was consistent with God's law.
The problem is deeper.
He recognized the people's disobedience without the narrative recording any acknowledgment of his own contribution to their exhaustion.
And then comes the verse that raises the central question.
“And Saul built an altar unto the LORD: the same was the first altar that he built unto the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 14:35, KJV
There it is.
The first altar Scripture records Saul building to the LORD.
After the exhausting oath.
After the desperate rush toward food.
After the violation of God's command.
After the rebuke.
Only then does the altar appear.
Why?
We need to distinguish carefully between what Scripture tells us and what it does not.

The passage does not explicitly say that Saul built the altar as a public-relations strategy. It does not state that the altar was a deliberate attempt to hide his failure. Nor does it reveal every thought behind his decision.
The immediate context shows Saul correcting the improper slaughter and consumption of the animals. The altar belongs to that moment of responding to the people's violation of God's law.
And although this is called his first altar to the LORD, that does not mean Saul had never previously participated in sacrifice or worship. Earlier passages record sacrifices during his reign.
But the placement of this first recorded altar is still spiritually sobering.
Because the story places Saul's religious action beside the consequences of his leadership.
It invites us to consider a question that reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
What happens when we become more concerned with correcting visible sin than confronting the pride, impatience, or foolishness that helped create the crisis?
Perhaps you have lived on the receiving end of that kind of leadership.
You were trying your best.
You were carrying responsibilities nobody noticed.
You were exhausted, overwhelmed, and quietly falling apart.
Then you made a mistake.
And suddenly, the people who had never asked why you were struggling became very interested in telling you what you had done wrong.
They saw the failure.
But they did not see the fatigue.
They saw the reaction.
But they did not see the pressure.
They saw the moment you stumbled.
But they did not see how long you had been trying to remain standing.
Maybe it happened in your family.
Maybe at work.
Maybe even in a church.
And perhaps you still carry the wound of being corrected by someone who never stopped to understand what you were carrying.
But this passage is not only for people who have been hurt by leaders.
It is also for those of us who have hurt others while believing we were doing what was right.
A father can demand respect while making his children afraid to speak honestly.
A mother can insist on obedience while failing to notice that her child is emotionally exhausted.
A ministry leader can demand constant service while neglecting the spiritual and physical well-being of volunteers.
A Christian can quote Scripture accurately while applying it without patience, tenderness, or wisdom.
And any of us can become so focused on the wrongdoing in front of us that we stop examining what is happening inside us.
That does not mean truth should be compromised.
It means truth must never become an excuse for lovelessness.
The Bible does not give us permission to replace God's commands with our personal preferences and then treat every struggle against those preferences as rebellion against God.
Saul's oath was not the same thing as God's law concerning blood.
One came from the king.
The other came from the LORD.
And confusing human demands with divine commands can wound the very people we are supposed to serve.
There is something else we must notice.
Saul's oath was not simply harsh. It was unnecessary to the victory God had already begun to accomplish.
Jonathan's faith had moved him to act because he trusted God's power.
Saul's oath placed the army under a restriction that weakened them.
What a contrast.
One man trusted that God could save with few.
The other tried to intensify the pursuit through a curse that left his soldiers hungry.
And the tragedy became even more personal when Saul's own son was nearly condemned under that oath.
Later in the chapter, Saul was prepared to see Jonathan die because Jonathan had unknowingly eaten the honey.
But the people intervened, recognizing that God had worked through Jonathan that day (1 Samuel 14:43–45).
The same chapter that records God's deliverance also reveals how dangerously Saul's judgment had become entangled with his own declarations.
That is why this is not merely a story about soldiers eating blood.
It is a story about what happens when a leader's will begins to overshadow the well-being of the people entrusted to him.
And it asks a question every Christian should take seriously.
Am I helping people obey God, or am I exhausting them with expectations God never placed upon them?
There is a difference between calling someone to repentance and crushing someone beneath your control.
There is a difference between spiritual discipline and spiritual pride.
There is a difference between honoring God's holiness and using religious language to protect your own authority.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment comes when we can no longer recognize that difference.
Because we can build altars.
We can attend worship.
We can quote Scripture.
We can correct others.
We can serve in ministry.
We can appear deeply religious.
And still need to repent of the way we have treated people.
An altar does not automatically prove a surrendered heart.
Religious activity cannot substitute for obedience.
Later, in 1 Samuel 15, after Saul again failed to obey God's instruction, Samuel confronted him with words that illuminate the larger pattern of his reign.
“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” — 1 Samuel 15:22, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “to obey” is שְׁמֹעַ (shemoa'), related to the verb shama', meaning to hear or listen, often with the implication of responding obediently.
God was not rejecting the sacrificial system He had established.
He was exposing the emptiness of sacrifice offered as a substitute for listening to Him.
And that distinction reaches into our own lives.
You cannot repair a pattern of cruelty simply by singing louder on Sunday.
You cannot justify dishonesty by giving generously.
You cannot replace repentance with public religious performance.
You cannot continually wound people and assume that spiritual activity makes the wounds insignificant.
God desires truth in the inward parts.
He calls us not merely to look holy but to belong to Him.
And that is where this story becomes more than a warning about Saul.
It becomes a mirror.
Because before we point toward the king and say, “How could he do that?” we need to ask whether we have ever done something similar.
Have you ever corrected someone harshly because you were embarrassed by their mistake?
Have you ever demanded patience while refusing to be patient?
Have you ever expected grace for your own failures but immediate consequences for everyone else's?
Have you ever defended your decisions so fiercely that you could no longer hear the pain of those affected by them?
Have you ever been more concerned with appearing right than becoming right before God?
Those questions hurt.
They should.
Not because God delights in humiliating us.
But because conviction can become a doorway to repentance.
And repentance is not the end of hope.
It is where we stop defending what needs to be surrendered.
This is where the Gospel changes the direction of the story.
Because Saul is not the final king we are meant to look toward.
There is another King.
A King who never confused His Father's will with selfish ambition.
A King who did not place needless religious burdens upon the weary.
A King who saw the exhausted, the hungry, the guilty, and the broken.
And instead of exploiting their weakness, He moved toward them with truth and compassion.
His name is Jesus Christ.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — KJV
Look at the difference.
Saul's command left his soldiers faint.
Jesus calls the weary to Himself.
Saul spoke of avenging himself upon his enemies.
Jesus willingly laid down His life for sinners.
Saul's leadership exposed the danger of human pride.
Jesus revealed the perfection of humble obedience.
Philippians 2:8 says that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
He did not merely teach obedience.
He embodied it.
He did not merely identify human sin.
He bore the judgment our sin deserved.
And unlike an earthly king who may overlook his own failures while condemning others, Jesus is the sinless Savior who sees every hidden thing and still invites sinners to repent and come to Him.
But do not misunderstand His compassion.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He does not excuse sin because we were tired, wounded, pressured, or afraid.
He tells us the truth about our condition.
And then He offers something no human altar, religious performance, or self-justifying explanation could ever provide.
Forgiveness through His finished work.
The book of Hebrews declares that Christ entered the holy place by His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12).
The blood Israel was forbidden to consume pointed to the sacredness of life and the seriousness of atonement within the old covenant.
The sacrifices of that covenant prepared the way for understanding the greater sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
His blood was not shed because He had sinned.
It was shed because we had.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7, KJV
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that our failures do not matter.
Not that leaders are never accountable.
Not that our wounds give us permission to disobey God.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, including those who have been wounded by others and those who must face the painful truth that they have wounded others.
Some of us need healing from the burdens people placed upon us.
Some of us need repentance for the burdens we placed upon others.
And some of us need both.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has been spiritually exhausted for years.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
Tired of pretending that you never struggle.
Tired of feeling as though every weakness makes you a disappointment.
Tired of being afraid that if people knew what was really happening inside you, they would stop treating you with kindness.
Hear this carefully.
You do not have to pretend that you are strong before coming to Christ.
You must come honestly.
Confess your sin where you have sinned.
Seek help where you are wounded.
Lay down the impossible burden of earning a salvation that only grace can give.
Jesus does not promise a life without obedience, sacrifice, or suffering.
He calls us to take up our cross and follow Him.
But He is not a careless master who invents burdens to satisfy His ego.
He is the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
And maybe you are reading this from the other side.
Maybe you have been the Saul in someone's story.
You had authority.
You had influence.
You believed you were protecting what was right.
But now you are beginning to recognize that your words wounded people.
Your expectations exhausted them.
Your pride made it difficult for you to apologize.
You corrected their failures while refusing to acknowledge your own.
If that is you, do not turn away from the conviction.
Do not rush to defend yourself.
Do not build another outward display of spirituality to avoid dealing with what God is exposing within.
Go to Jesus.
Repent.
Where possible and appropriate, acknowledge the harm you caused.
Ask forgiveness without demanding it.
Make restitution where it is needed.
Change the way you lead.
Let your repentance become visible through humility, truthfulness, and a different way of treating people.
Because genuine repentance is not merely feeling bad that something happened.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And the grace of Christ is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the power and mercy through which forgiven sinners begin to walk in newness of life.
Perhaps that is the deepest warning in Saul's first recorded altar.
You can recognize the sin around you and still be blind to the repentance needed within you.
And perhaps the deepest hope is this:
Jesus is able to open our eyes before our pride destroys what has been entrusted to us.
So before you finish reading, consider one question.
What altar are you building to avoid an apology you need to make?
What religious activity are you using to distract yourself from an act of obedience God is calling you to?
What burden have you placed upon someone that you need to lift?
Or what burden have you been carrying that was never God's command in the first place?
Do not rush past those questions.
Bring them before the Lord.
Let His Word examine you.
And remember that the purpose of conviction is not to drive the repentant sinner into hopelessness.
It is to lead us toward the Savior whose mercy is greater than our excuses, whose holiness is greater than our self-righteousness, and whose grace is sufficient to transform a surrendered life.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person wrestling with these things.
Because one day you may need to return to this passage—not to examine someone else's failures, but to remember the kind of servant Christ is calling you to become.

And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, you are invited to walk with us as we continue sharing Scripture, biblical encouragement, honest conviction, and the transforming hope of Jesus Christ.
Not to build a following around a human personality.
But to keep directing attention toward the Savior who alone can redeem sinners.
There is also something I want to share with those who believe this kind of Gospel-centered work should continue reaching more people.
Writing, publishing, maintaining resources, and making biblical discipleship material accessible requires time, effort, and financial support.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
We honor those responsibilities.
The Gospel is free.
God's grace cannot be bought.
These resources and products are not the foundation of anyone's faith.
Christ is.
They are simply ways to encourage believers, carry biblical reminders into everyday life, and help sustain the ministry's ongoing work.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite your family and friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even people who do not yet believe, to read the Scriptures and consider the claims of Jesus Christ.
Follow along.
Join the conversations.
Encourage someone who is weary.
A single sincere conversation about the Gospel can matter more than we realize.
Because that is what Saul's story should ultimately drive us toward.
Not admiration for religious performance.
Not fear of human authority.
Not a life spent hiding behind spiritual appearances.
But surrender to the true King.
The One who never sinned.
The One who obeyed the Father perfectly.
The One who carried our guilt to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls the proud to repentance and the weary to rest.
Saul built an altar after the damage was done.
But Jesus Christ gave Himself as the perfect sacrifice to deal with the deepest damage sin has done to us all.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your failure began.
Your pride can be confronted.
Your sin can be forgiven.
Your wounds can be brought before the Savior.
Your life can be changed.
Not because you finally learned how to appear holy.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
The altar Saul built could not undo the wounds his leadership had caused—but the cross of Jesus Christ still calls wounded people and repentant sinners home.
